newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Antwerp bourse, world's oldest, set to disappear.
newsitem.headline: Antwerp bourse, world's oldest, set to disappear.

text.p: Belgium's Antwerp stock exchange, the world's oldest bourse founded in 1531, is set to disappear under proposals to merge it with the much larger Brussels bourse, officials said on Thursday.
"The Antwerp bourse has done its task. Fundamentally, we are moving in the direction of a merger of the Antwerp bourse into the Brussels bourse," chairman Marc Corluy told Reuters.
The officials said the boards of the two exchanges held discussions on Thursday on several proposals to increase cooperation between the two exchanges.
Brussels bourse deputy director Anne Vleminckx told Reuters its board had authorised management to discuss "intense cooperation" between the two exchanges. "Nothing has been signed so far," she said.
But Antwerp bourse officials made clear the aim was for the Antwerp bourse to be swallowed up by its larger neighbour.

"It makes no economic sense to have two stock exchanges (in Belgium). The idea is that the Antwerp bourse would lose its status as a stock exchange, although our offices and personnel would continue to act as a regional service centre in the coming years," Antwerp bourse director Fonne Hendrickx told Reuters.
He said he hoped there would be an agreement on a merger by the end of the year.

At the end of 1996, total market capitalisation in the few local shares traded on the Antwerp bourse stood at 15 billion belgian francs ($443 million), just a fraction of the more than 3,000 billion franc capitalisation of the Brussels bourse.

The Antwerp exchange building was built in 1531 and was the first public building used exclusively for financial and commodity trading. It served as a model for the London stock exchange building in the late 16th century and for the Amsterdam bourse, which was built in 1611.

The very word "bourse" -- in the sense of a place where traders meet to conduct financial affairs -- originated in Bruges, another northern Belgian town, and spread through Europe via Antwerp in the 16th and 17th centuries.
Variations on the 15th-century Dutch-language word "beurze" now stand for "financial exchange" in most European languages.
Antwerp's 1531 exchange hall still exists, though what little share trading there is left in the port city has moved to modern buildings nearby.
The two other Belgian regional bourses in Ghent and Liege were closed down in a national stock market reform of the early 1990s. ($1=33.83 Belgian Franc)
